title: How iGaming works
summary: How sportsbooks and casinos make money, how CPA, RevShare and hybrid deals turn that into your payout, and why only qualified FTDs count. You finish able to value a player, read operator KPIs and choose an offer with written rules before you spend.

lessons.title: Sportsbook and casino: two different businesses
objectives: By the end you can explain how a sportsbook and an online casino each make money.
You can turn betting odds into implied probability and the bookmaker's margin.
You can work out GGR and NGR from simple figures and see where your RevShare comes from.
You can say why the same number of FTDs can be worth very different amounts in each product.

steps.h: Why the product decides your money
steps.p: iGaming covers two different businesses: the sportsbook, where people bet on matches, and the casino, where people play slots and table games. They earn in different ways, keep players for different lengths of time and pay affiliates differently. If you promote both as if they were the same, you will misread your numbers and pick the wrong deal.
steps.more: Every number you will meet later in this school, from qualified FTD to RevShare to negative carryover, depends on how the operator earns. A sportsbook earns a margin built into the odds, so its results swing with match outcomes. A casino earns a house edge on every round, so its results are steadier per pound wagered but depend on how long a player keeps playing. This lesson gives you the mechanics in plain numbers so the rest of the school makes sense.

d.s: Understand the product before you price the traffic.

steps.say: iGaming is really two different businesses. The sportsbook, where people bet on matches, and the casino, where people play slots and table games. They earn in different ways, keep players for different lengths of time, and pay affiliates differently. Notice the line on screen: same F T D count, different value. F T D means first time deposit. A sportsbook's results swing with match outcomes, while a casino's are steadier per amount wagered. Understand the product before you price the traffic.

steps.p: A rough guide, varies by brand and geo. Many operators sell both under one account, but the law in your target country may only allow one of them, and the deal may pay differently for each.

Earns by|A margin built into the odds

steps.say: Here are the two products side by side, as a rough guide that varies by brand and geo. The sportsbook takes bets on football, basketball and other events, and earns through a margin built into the odds. Its rhythm spikes on match days and big tournaments. The casino covers slots, roulette, blackjack, live dealer and crash games, and earns a house edge on every round. Its rhythm is steadier, every day, every hour. Many operators sell both, but the law in your country may allow only one.

steps.p: Decimal odds show what a winning bet returns per unit staked, including the stake. Divide 1 by the odds to get the implied probability the bookmaker has priced in. Odds of 2.00 imply 50%. Odds of 1.90 imply about 52.6%.
d: Decimal odds
Implied probability
steps.say: Odds hide a probability. Decimal odds show what a winning bet returns per unit staked, including the stake. Follow the equation: one, divided by the decimal odds, gives the implied probability the bookmaker has priced in. So odds of two point nought nought imply fifty percent. Odds of one point nine nought imply about fifty two point six percent. That small difference is where the bookmaker's margin lives.

steps.p: Example. A two-way market where both sides are priced at 1.90. Add the implied probabilities and you get more than 100%. The extra is the overround. It is how the sportsbook earns no matter which side wins, as long as money is spread across both sides.
steps.more: Example maths: 1 ÷ 1.90 = 0.5263. Two sides give 1.0526, an overround of 5.26%. The bookmaker's theoretical hold is 1 − 1 ÷ 1.0526 = 0.05, or 5.0% of money staked. In practice the result of each match decides whether the book wins or loses that day, so real margins swing. Over thousands of bets the margin tends to show through, which is why sportsbook RevShare should be judged over months, not days.
steps.say: Here's a worked example of the bookmaker's margin. In a two-way market, both teams are priced at one point nine nought. Look at the table. Each side implies fifty two point six percent, so together they add up to about one hundred and five point three percent. That extra over one hundred is the overround. It works out to a theoretical margin of about five percent of money staked. In practice each match decides whether the book wins that day, so judge sportsbook RevShare over months, not days.

steps.p: Example. Players in your cohort stake ₦10,000,000 in a month at a 5% theoretical margin. The sportsbook expects about ₦500,000 of gross gaming revenue. If favourites keep winning, the real figure can be far lower or even negative for that month.

d.label: theoretical GGR on ₦10m staked
d.note: Example. Real results swing with match outcomes.

steps.say: Let's put that margin on real money. In this example, players in your cohort stake ten million naira in a month, at a five percent theoretical margin. The sportsbook expects about five hundred thousand naira of gross gaming revenue, or G G R. That's the number on screen. But notice the warning: if favourites keep winning, the real figure can be far lower, or even negative, for that month.

steps.p: Casino games publish or imply a return to player, RTP. A slot with 96% RTP pays back, over a very long run, 96 of every 100 staked. The other 4% is the house edge. Each spin is random, but the edge is built into every round.
d: RTP 96%
House edge 4%
steps.say: The casino's edge is called R T P, return to player. Follow the equation on screen: one hundred percent, minus an R T P of ninety six percent, equals a house edge of four percent. So a ninety six percent slot pays back, over a very long run, ninety six of every hundred staked. Each spin is random, but the edge is built into every single round.

steps.p: Example. A player deposits $20 and plays a 96% RTP slot at $0.50 a spin. Wins get re-staked, so the same money circulates. After 1,000 spins the player has staked $500 in total, and the expected loss is 4% of that.
steps.more: This is why turnover and deposits are different numbers. A $20 deposit can create $500 of bets because winnings are recycled. Operators report deposits, turnover, GGR and NGR, and your RevShare is usually paid on NGR, not on deposits. When a manager quotes you a big turnover figure, ask what the NGR was. Results per player vary hugely: some win and withdraw, others lose the deposit quickly.
steps.say: Here's one casino deposit, worked through. In this example, a player deposits twenty dollars and plays a ninety six percent slot at fifty cents a spin. Wins get re-staked, so the same money circulates. After one thousand spins, they've staked five hundred dollars in total. That's the turnover. At a four percent house edge, the expected G G R is twenty dollars. So turnover and deposits are very different numbers. When a manager quotes a big turnover figure, ask what the N G R, the net gaming revenue, was.

steps.h: How the two products move week to week
steps.p: Example cohort GGR over seven weeks. Sportsbook GGR jumps around with results, and can go negative in a week where favourites win. Casino GGR is smoother but fades as players stop. Illustrative shapes, not benchmarks.
steps.say: This chart shows how the two products move week to week, using an example cohort. The sportsbook line jumps around with results, and in week four it even goes negative, a week where favourites won. The casino line is smoother, but it fades steadily as players stop. These are illustrative shapes, not benchmarks. The point is that each product needs a different kind of patience.

steps.p: Gross gaming revenue is stakes minus winnings paid. Net gaming revenue is what is left after the deductions your contract allows, usually bonuses, gaming taxes and some fees. RevShare is almost always a percentage of NGR, so the deductions matter as much as the percentage.
d: GGR
Bonuses, taxes, fees
NGR
steps.say: Now from G G R to N G R. Gross gaming revenue is stakes minus winnings paid. Net gaming revenue, N G R, is what's left after the deductions your contract allows, usually bonuses, gaming taxes and some fees. Follow the equation: G G R, minus bonuses, taxes and fees, equals N G R. RevShare is almost always a percentage of N G R, so the deductions matter as much as the percentage.

steps.h: Worked example: your RevShare from NGR
steps.p: Example. Your players produce $1,000 GGR in a month. The contract lets the operator deduct bonuses, gaming tax and payment fees. You are on 30% RevShare. Read your own contract: the list of deductions differs between operators.
steps.more: Notice that a 30% share of GGR would have been $300, but a 30% share of NGR is $180. Two deals that both say 30% can pay very different amounts. Some contracts also deduct an admin or platform fee as a percentage, and some cap deductions. Ask for the exact NGR formula in writing before you compare offers.
steps.say: Here's a worked example of RevShare from N G R. Your players produce one thousand dollars G G R in a month. Read down the table. Bonuses used take off two hundred, gaming tax one hundred and fifty, and payment fees fifty. That leaves six hundred dollars N G R. At thirty percent, you earn one hundred and eighty dollars. Notice that thirty percent of G G R would have been three hundred. So two deals that both say thirty percent can pay very differently. Ask for the exact formula in writing.

steps.p: The player stakes with the operator. The operator's results, after deductions, create NGR. The network or affiliate programme reports it and pays you your share or your CPA. You earn only because of the operator's earnings, which come from players' net losses.
steps.say: This map shows where the money flows. Start at your ad. It sends a click to an adult player. The player deposits and bets with a licensed operator. The operator's results go through the G G R to N G R step. The network or programme reports it, and pays you your C P A, cost per acquisition, or your share. Follow the arrows and you'll see it: you earn only because the operator earns, and that comes from players' net losses.

lessons.title: CPA, RevShare and hybrid: the maths
objectives: By the end you can model what 100 FTDs pay under CPA, RevShare and hybrid deals.
You can work out a break-even cost per FTD for a RevShare deal over a time horizon.
You can explain why cash flow, not the 12-month total, often decides the right deal.
You can choose a deal type with written starting rules.

steps.h: Why the deal type matters as much as the traffic
steps.p: Two buyers can send identical traffic and end the year with very different results because one took CPA and the other took RevShare. The deal decides when you get paid, how much risk you carry and whether you survive a slow month. Get this wrong and good traffic can still sink your bankroll.

d.s: Model the deal before you buy a single click.

steps.say: Two buyers can send identical traffic and end the year with very different results, because one took C P A, cost per acquisition, and the other took RevShare. The deal decides when you get paid, how much risk you carry, and whether you survive a slow month. As the screen says: same players, three different paydays. Model the deal before you buy a single click.

steps.p: These are the shapes you will meet most. Names and details vary by programme, and a deal can mix tiers, caps and bonuses on top. Always ask for the exact terms in writing.
d: CPA|A fixed fee per qualified FTD, paid once
RevShare|A % of the NGR your players produce, paid monthly for as long as the deal says
Hybrid|A smaller CPA plus a smaller RevShare
Tiered|Payout rises when you pass a monthly volume
steps.say: Here are the three common deal types, plus one extra. C P A is a fixed fee per qualified F T D, first time deposit, paid once. RevShare is a percentage of the N G R, net gaming revenue, your players produce, paid monthly for as long as the deal says. Hybrid is a smaller C P A plus a smaller RevShare. And tiered means the payout rises when you pass a monthly volume. Names and details vary by programme, so always ask for the exact terms in writing.

steps.p: Example. 100 qualified FTDs from one month of buying. The operator's data for similar players shows how much NGR each FTD produces over time. These figures are illustrative, not benchmarks; ask your programme for its own cohort data.
steps.more: Example maths: months 4 to 12 are nine months at $5, which is $45. Add months 1 to 3 ($55) and the 12-month NGR per FTD is $100. Real cohorts are lumpier: a few players produce most of the NGR, and in sportsbook a single bad month for the operator can be negative. We use smooth numbers here so you can follow the maths.
steps.say: Now the assumptions for our model. In this example, one hundred qualified F T Ds come from one month of buying. Read the table. Each F T D produces thirty dollars N G R in month one, fifteen in month two, ten in month three, then five dollars a month from month four to twelve. That adds up to one hundred dollars over twelve months. These are illustrative, smooth numbers so you can follow the maths. Real cohorts are lumpier, so ask your programme for its own data.

steps.h: Worked example: what each deal pays
steps.p: Example. Same 100 FTDs under three deals: CPA $40; RevShare 35%; hybrid $20 CPA plus 20% RevShare. Look at month 1, month 3 and month 12 separately. The totals tell one story; the timing tells another.
steps.more: Working. CPA: 100 × $40 = $4,000. RevShare month 1: 100 × $30 × 35% = $1,050. By month 3: 100 × $55 × 35% = $1,925. By month 12: 100 × $100 × 35% = $3,500. Hybrid month 1: 100 × $20 = $2,000 plus 100 × $30 × 20% = $600, so $2,600. By month 3: $2,000 + 100 × $55 × 20% = $3,100. By month 12: $2,000 + 100 × $100 × 20% = $4,000. Payment timing also depends on your net terms, often paid after month close.
steps.say: Here's what each deal pays on those hundred F T Ds. Look at the three columns: month one, by month three, and by month twelve. C P A at forty dollars pays four thousand dollars, all upfront. RevShare at thirty five percent pays one thousand and fifty in month one, one thousand nine hundred and twenty five by month three, and three thousand five hundred by month twelve. The hybrid, twenty dollars plus twenty percent, pays two thousand six hundred, then three thousand one hundred, then four thousand. The totals tell one story. The timing tells another.

steps.p: Example, 100 FTDs. CPA pays everything early. RevShare starts low and climbs slowly. In this example it never catches CPA within 12 months. With longer-lived players, or a higher share, it can overtake later.
steps.say: This curve shows the cumulative payout. The flat line is C P A, four thousand dollars, paid early. The rising line is RevShare at thirty five percent. It starts low and climbs slowly. In this example, it never catches C P A within twelve months. With longer-lived players or a higher share, it could overtake later. So don't assume RevShare always wins in the end.

steps.h: Break-even cost per FTD on RevShare
steps.p: On RevShare, the most you can pay for an FTD and break even is the NGR per FTD you expect over your chosen horizon times your share. Pick the horizon by how long you can wait for cash, not by how far a spreadsheet can stretch.
steps.more: Example. 12-month horizon: $100 × 35% = $35. 3-month horizon: $55 × 35% = $19.25. If you buy FTDs at $30, you are profitable on paper over 12 months but you are $10.75 per FTD underwater at month 3. That gap is money you must fund from your own bankroll while you wait.
d: NGR per FTD (horizon)
RevShare %
Break-even CPFTD
steps.say: How much can you pay per F T D on RevShare and still break even? Follow the equation: the N G R per F T D over your chosen horizon, times your RevShare percentage. In this example, over twelve months, one hundred dollars times thirty five percent is thirty five dollars. Over three months, it's only nineteen dollars twenty five. So if you pay thirty dollars per F T D, you're fine on paper at twelve months, but underwater at month three. Choose the horizon by how long you can wait for cash.

steps.h: Cash you must fund on RevShare
steps.p: Example. You buy 100 FTDs at $30 each, $3,000 spent. After three months RevShare has paid $1,925. You are still $1,075 short and must keep funding new campaigns from your own money.
steps.say: This is the cash you must fund on RevShare. In this example, you buy one hundred F T Ds at thirty dollars each, three thousand dollars spent. After three months, RevShare has paid one thousand nine hundred and twenty five. So you're still one thousand and seventy five dollars short, the number on screen. Meanwhile, you must keep funding new campaigns from your own money.

steps.p: A rough guide. RevShare gives you a share of the upside and also of the operator's problems. These are the risks to price in before you accept a pure RevShare deal.
steps.more: Negative carryover means a negative NGR month is carried forward and deducted from future positive months before you earn again. Many programmes have policies on this; some reset monthly, some carry forward indefinitely. We cover it in depth in the scaling module. For now: ask whether it applies and how, before you sign.
steps.say: RevShare gives you a share of the upside, and also of the operator's problems. Read the table as a rough guide. A big player win can make N G R negative, and no negative carryover protects you. Deduction changes shrink your N G R, so get a fixed formula in your contract. If a brand exits the geo, income stops, so spread across brands. A few whales make income lumpy, so use larger samples. And late payments create a cash gap, so insist on clear net terms.

steps.h: Worked example: projected CPA while you wait
steps.p: Example. Target CPA $35 on qualified FTDs, payout $50. Day 3: $105 spent, 4 FTDs, none qualified yet. Your history says 70% of FTDs qualify. Use that rate to project, then apply the rule card to the projected CPA.
steps.more: Example rules used: kill at spend ≥ 2 × target with 0 conversions; kill when CPA is above the lower of 1.5 × target and break-even once spend reaches 3 × target; scale +20% when CPA ≤ 0.8 × target with at least 3 conversions. Here 1.5 × $35 = $52.50, break-even is the $50 payout, so the kill line is $50. $105 is exactly 3 × target, and $37.50 is under $50, so you hold. When your qualified rate is unknown, use 60% as a cautious starting assumption and replace it with real data after the first month close.
steps.say: Here's how to use a projected C P A while you wait. In this example, your target is thirty five dollars, payout fifty. steps.h: Why player value sets your ceiling
steps.p: On RevShare, the value of a player decides the most you can pay to get them. On CPA, the operator uses the same value to decide how much to pay you, and whether to keep paying. If you understand player value, you can negotiate, choose geos and spot bad traffic before the operator does.

steps.say: Why does player value matter so much? On RevShare, the value of a player decides the most you can pay to get them. On C P A, cost per acquisition, the operator uses that same value to decide how much to pay you, and whether to keep paying. As the screen says, both you and the operator are doing this maths. Understand it, and you can negotiate, choose geos, and spot bad traffic before the operator does.

steps.p: NGR per FTD comes from a few drivers. Each one is something you can ask the operator about and something your traffic choices can change, for better or worse.
d: Deposits per player|How often they deposit in the period
Average deposit|Size of each deposit

steps.say: N G R, net gaming revenue, per F T D, first time deposit, comes from a few drivers. Look at the cards. Deposits per player, how often they deposit. Average deposit, the size of each one. Hold on deposits, the G G R, gross gaming revenue, as a share of deposits. The N G R ratio, what's left after bonuses and taxes. And retention, how many are still active after weeks. You can ask the operator about each one, and your traffic choices can change each one, for better or worse.

steps.h: NGR per FTD from its drivers

steps.say: To get N G R per F T D, multiply the drivers together. Follow the equation: deposits times average deposit, times G G R over deposits, times N G R over G G R. Each one is an average across the cohort, so the result is an average too. Averages are useful for planning, but dangerous for small samples, as you'll see next.

steps.p: Example. 200 FTDs in Kenya. Over 90 days each makes 4.2 deposits on average, averaging $22. The operator holds 30% of deposits as GGR, and NGR is 70% of GGR after bonuses and tax. You are on 35% RevShare.

If you could get a $30 CPA for the same players, CPA would pay over four times more in that window. RevShare only wins if players keep producing NGR for many months after day 90, which is why you need the operator's longer cohort data. All figures here are examples.

steps.p: For RevShare, set your maximum cost per FTD from a cautious value, not a hopeful one. Use NGR per FTD over the horizon you can afford, times your share, times a safety factor below 1 to cover estimate error and slow payment.
